description: I’m a solo builder interested in where software meets hardware: sensors, processors, and the models that interpret what they measure. Cabin air is a clear example of that gap. A sensor reads one spot, and software has to work out the rest. I built CALYPSO to make that gap visible and to help crews act on it.
summary:
In microgravity, exhaled CO₂ doesn’t drift away from an astronaut’s face. It pools there, while wall-mounted sensors still read normal. CALYPSO is a cabin air simulator that shows what fixed sensors miss and what a crew can do about it.

Adjust ventilation, CO₂ scrubbing, the O₂ regulator or crew activity and watch a two-compartment model (breathing zone and main cabin) respond in real time. Use the Sensor Lab to test where a sensor should be placed. Then open the Crew Exposure map to see how the air affects seven body systems. Real NASA RR-1 flight and ground data (CO₂, temperature, humidity) sits next to the model, and Roger, a built-in AI assistant, helps you read each scenario.
details: In microgravity, poor airflow lets exhaled CO₂ pocket and O₂ dip near astronauts' faces while fixed wall sensors miss the buildup. I created CALYPSO (calypso-tan.vercel.app) to make this hidden life-support risk visible and testable for students, educators, and researchers. Built with JavaScript, HTML/CSS, GitHub, and Vercel, it runs a real-time two-compartment Forward Euler ODE simulation tracking gas exchange between a modeled breathing zone and the main cabin. Users can adjust ventilation, CO₂ scrubbing, O₂ regulators, and crew activity; test sensor placement in the Sensor Lab; explore physiological impacts across seven body systems on the Crew Exposure map; inspect real NASA RR-1 flight and ground datasets (CO₂, temperature, humidity); review transparent equations in Research & Methods; export or share scenario reports; and consult Roger, our built-in AI lab partner. We prioritized scientific transparency by clearly separating educational demo rules from NASA clinical limits.
